static.topic: Israel–Palestine Conflict and the West Asia Peace Process
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India's interests; bilateral and regional developments affecting India
static.whatIsIt: The long-running dispute over sovereignty and statehood in historic Palestine, centred on Israel's occupation of the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza and on Palestinian claims to statehood. Since October 2023 the Gaza Strip has been the theatre of a large-scale Israeli military campaign, and repeated incidents around aid distribution have drawn scrutiny under international humanitarian law.
static.background: UNGA Resolution 181 (1947) proposed partition; Israel declared independence in 1948, triggering the first Arab-Israeli war; UNSC Resolution 242 (1967) after the Six-Day War laid down the land-for-peace principle; the Oslo Accords (1993) created the Palestinian Authority; the Second Intifada began in 2000; Hamas took control of Gaza in 2007; major Gaza wars followed in 2008-09, 2012, 2014 and 2021, and a further war began after the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023. The two-state solution remains the internationally endorsed framework.
static.geography: Levant, eastern Mediterranean: Israel, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Gaza Strip; Gaza is a narrow coastal strip of roughly 365 sq km bordering Israel and Egypt, with the Rafah crossing as its main non-Israeli gateway.
static.socioEconomic: Gaza's economy is heavily aid-dependent, with high unemployment and severe restrictions on the movement of people and goods; food insecurity, destroyed infrastructure and reliance on humanitarian convoys are central to the present crisis.
static.whyInNews: Witnesses said an Israeli strike on 21 November 2026 hit a vehicle distributing aid in Gaza, killing three people and leaving food scattered at the scene, alongside parallel political flux in Israel.
static.wayForward: Revive a credible political process towards a two-state solution; secure unimpeded humanitarian access and protection of aid workers and civilians; pursue regional de-escalation, with India continuing to back Palestinian statehood and Israeli security.
prelimsPointers: UNGA Resolution 181 (1947) proposed the partition of Palestine; UNSC Resolution 242 (1967) set out the land-for-peace principle.
India recognised the State of Palestine in 1988 and supports a two-state solution.
static.mainsAngle: Balancing Israel's security concerns against Palestinian statehood and humanitarian-law obligations in asymmetric conflict — examine the viability of the two-state framework.

static.topic: United Nations and Multilateral Reform
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Important international institutions, agencies and fora and their structure, mandate
static.whatIsIt: The UN (1945) has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members. India has long sought permanent UNSC membership and is one of the largest troop contributors to UN peacekeeping.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and a leading peacekeeping contributor. The G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) campaigns for expansion of the Council; the Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) on Security Council reform remain inconclusive, with the African Ezulwini Consensus also demanding permanent representation.
static.geography: UN Headquarters is in New York; the International Court of Justice sits at The Hague.
static.whyInNews: Contested Security Council action on Gaza and repeated veto use have renewed debate on UNSC composition, working methods and credibility — the backdrop to India's claim for permanent membership.
static.wayForward: Move the IGN to text-based negotiations; expand both permanent and non-permanent categories; accommodate the African position; improve working methods, including restraint on the veto in mass-atrocity situations.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent (China, France, Russia, UK, US) with veto power plus 10 elected for two-year terms.
The ICJ is at The Hague; the UN Headquarters is in New York.
static.mainsAngle: India's claim to permanent UNSC membership rests on representativeness, population and peacekeeping contributions — assess the obstacles posed by veto politics and the Ezulwini Consensus.

static.topic: India–Israel Relations
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Bilateral relations; India's West Asia outreach and de-hyphenation
static.whatIsIt: India–Israel relations, formalised as full diplomatic ties in 1992, cover defence procurement, agriculture and water technology, homeland security, cyber and innovation, while India simultaneously maintains its long-standing support for the Palestinian cause.
static.background: India voted against Israel's creation in 1947 and recognised Israel in 1950 but had no full diplomatic ties until 1992. Defence and strategic cooperation deepened through the Kargil conflict (1999) and the following decade; Prime Minister Narendra Modi's 2017 visit was the first by an Indian Prime Minister; the I2U2 grouping (India, Israel, UAE, US) was launched in 2022. India follows a policy of 'de-hyphenation', engaging Israel and Palestine on separate tracks.
static.geography: Israel lies on the eastern Mediterranean, bordering Lebanon, Syria, Jordan and Egypt; West Asia connectivity initiatives such as the proposed India–Middle East–Europe corridor would run through the region.
static.socioEconomic: Bilateral trade is modest relative to the strategic weight of the relationship; India is among Israel's significant defence export customers, and agri-tech such as drip irrigation and desalination features prominently in cooperation.
static.whyInNews: Election-year flux in Israel — Eisenkot's Yashar inviting Netanyahu's Likud to coalition talks — bears on the continuity of India's engagements, even as the Gaza war shapes India's balancing between Israel and Palestine.
static.wayForward: Continue de-hyphenated engagement, deepen technology and defence ties, press for humanitarian access in Gaza, and keep the two-state solution at the core of India's West Asia diplomacy.
prelimsPointers: India established full diplomatic relations with Israel in 1992, having recognised Israel in 1950.
India recognised the State of Palestine in 1988 and has consistently voted for Palestinian rights at the UN.
static.mainsAngle: Assess the de-hyphenation doctrine in India's West Asia policy and its durability amid the Gaza conflict and shifting Israeli coalition politics.

prelims: Israel's legislature, the Knesset, has 120 members; a coalition needs 61 seats for a majority.
Likud is led by Benjamin Netanyahu; the Yashar party is chaired by Gadi Eisenkot, as reported in the coverage.
UNSC has 15 members — five permanent veto-wielding members and ten elected for two-year terms.
The Gaza Strip covers about 365 sq km and borders Israel and Egypt, with Rafah as its main non-Israeli crossing.
stories.mainsQuestion: Coalition flux in Israel and continuing strikes in Gaza show how domestic politics and active conflict reinforce each other in West Asia. Examine the implications for India's West Asia policy and for the rules-based international order.

stories.headline: Sri Lanka's organised crime bill clears Supreme Court constitutional scrutiny
stories.summary: Sri Lanka's proposed organised crime legislation has cleared scrutiny by its Supreme Court, removing a key constitutional hurdle before enactment. The Bill had attracted 20 petitions challenging its constitutionality, reflecting the island nation's distinctive pre-enactment review mechanism under which citizens may petition the Supreme Court within one week of a Bill's introduction in Parliament. The clearance allows the government to proceed with a law aimed at strengthening the legal framework against organised crime. The episode illustrates how constitutional courts can shape security legislation before it formally becomes law, a route unavailable in India, where judicial review operates after enactment.
stories.whyItMatters: Offers a comparative constitutional angle on pre-enactment versus post-enactment judicial review, useful for GS-II polity questions on judicial review and legislative process. Also relevant to GS-II international relations as a neighbourhood and Indian Ocean development.

perspectives.take: Reports the Supreme Court clearance factually, foregrounding the 20 constitutional petitions and Sri Lanka's one-week window for citizens to challenge a Bill — a neutral, procedural framing typical of its international coverage.

articles.title: Sri Lanka's organised crime bill gets Supreme Court nod
articles.snippet: In Sri Lanka, citizens can challenge a Bill's constitutionality in the Supreme Court within one week of its introduction in Parliament. The Bill had earlier faced 20 petitions in the Supreme Court challenging its constitutionality

static.topic: Pre-enactment judicial review of legislation
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary: Judicial Review and Constitutional Courts
static.whatIsIt: Pre-enactment review allows a Bill's constitutionality to be tested in the apex court before it becomes law. In Sri Lanka, citizens may challenge a Bill in the Supreme Court within one week of its introduction in Parliament — the route used by the 20 petitions against the organised crime Bill.
static.background: Sri Lanka's constitutional scheme provides for such advance scrutiny, unlike India, where courts test a law after enactment through writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 (Supreme Court) and 226 (High Courts). India's basic-structure doctrine, established in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), permits invalidation of constitutional amendments that damage the Constitution's essential features. The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998), and PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s.
static.geography: South Asia; Sri Lanka is a neighbouring Indian Ocean state separated from India by the Palk Strait and Gulf of Mannar.
static.socioEconomic: Organised crime legislation typically targets extortion, drug trafficking and gang networks, and its design raises questions about surveillance powers, due process and individual liberties.
static.whyInNews: Sri Lanka's organised crime Bill cleared Supreme Court scrutiny after facing 20 petitions challenging its constitutionality.
static.wayForward: Comparative study of pre-enactment and post-enactment review can inform debate on reducing litigation delays while preserving constitutional safeguards.
prelimsPointers: In Sri Lanka, a Bill's constitutionality can be challenged in the Supreme Court within one week of its introduction in Parliament.
In India, judicial review operates after enactment; there is no equivalent one-week pre-enactment window.
Articles 32 and 226 empower the Supreme Court and High Courts respectively to issue writs.
static.mainsAngle: Compare pre-enactment and post-enactment judicial review and assess which better balances parliamentary sovereignty with constitutional supremacy.

static.topic: Parliament, Legislation and Bills
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Parliament and Legislative Process
static.whatIsIt: A Bill becomes law after passage by both Houses and Presidential assent (Article 111). Parliament under Article 79 comprises the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha.
static.background: Money Bills (Article 110) originate only in the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha may delay but not amend their money provisions. Ordinances (Article 123) may be promulgated when Parliament is not in session and must be approved within six weeks of reassembly. Departmentally Related Standing Committees scrutinise Bills.
static.whyInNews: The Sri Lankan organised crime Bill's passage through Parliament and the pre-enactment challenge illustrate how legislative and judicial stages interact in a neighbouring parliamentary democracy.
static.wayForward: Strengthening committee referral and scrutiny improves the quality of legislation and reduces the need for later judicial correction.
prelimsPointers: A no-confidence motion can be moved only in the Lok Sabha.
Adjournment, prorogation and dissolution differ in their effect on pending Bills; a Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses on Lok Sabha dissolution only if not yet passed by the Lok Sabha.
static.mainsAngle: Assess declining legislative scrutiny and committee referrals, and treat parliamentary productivity as a governance indicator.

static.topic: India's Neighbourhood Policy and the Indian Ocean
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and the World
static.whatIsIt: India's foreign policy combines strategic autonomy, multi-alignment, and the Neighbourhood First and Act East outlooks, engaging simultaneously with the Quad, BRICS, SCO, G20 and IBSA.
static.background: Rooted in NAM (1961) and Panchsheel (1954), the policy was reshaped by post-1991 liberalisation and the 1998 nuclear tests. The Indo-Pacific concept and the Quad, with the US, Japan and Australia, gained salience after 2017.
static.geography: Indian Ocean neighbourhood; Sri Lanka lies across the Palk Strait and Gulf of Mannar, close to key sea lanes.
static.socioEconomic: India–Sri Lanka ties span trade, connectivity, energy and security cooperation, making stability in the island nation relevant to regional economic and maritime interests.
static.whyInNews: Developments in Sri Lanka's domestic law-and-order framework bear on India's neighbourhood and Indian Ocean security interests.
static.wayForward: Sustained engagement under Neighbourhood First, with attention to maritime security and people-centric connectivity, serves India's regional interests.
prelimsPointers: India assumed the G20 presidency in 2022–23; the African Union was admitted as a permanent G20 member in 2023.
India and Pakistan joined the SCO in 2017.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how India balances ties with the West, Russia and the Global South while acting as a bridging power in its neighbourhood.

prelims: Sri Lanka permits citizens to challenge a Bill's constitutionality in the Supreme Court within one week of its introduction in Parliament.
The organised crime Bill faced 20 such petitions before receiving Supreme Court clearance.
India has no equivalent pre-enactment review window; its courts test legislation after enactment under Articles 32 and 226.
stories.mainsQuestion: Pre-enactment judicial review, as practised in Sri Lanka, is often contrasted with India's post-enactment model. Examine the merits and demerits of both approaches in reconciling parliamentary sovereignty with constitutional supremacy.

stories.headline: Data centres' water footprint extends beyond onsite cooling to the power grid
stories.summary: A study reported by Scroll.in finds that although data centre operators may cut the water consumed at their own campuses for cooling, they generally do not account for the water used to generate the electricity those facilities draw from the grid. Data centres therefore carry two water footprints — a direct onsite one from evaporative cooling systems, and an indirect offsite one arising from water-intensive thermal power generation. This matters because India's data centre clusters sit in and around cities and districts that are already water-stressed, and because water is largely a State subject governed mainly through groundwater permits rather than resource-disclosure norms. The finding pushes back against judging a facility's water performance solely on onsite metrics such as Water Usage Effectiveness, since site-level efficiency need not reduce pressure on the basin or the grid that supplies it.
stories.whyItMatters: Directly usable in GS-III answers on the energy–water nexus, environmental accounting of the digital economy and industrial water regulation, and in GS-I geography on water resources and GS-II on state capacity to regulate new-economy infrastructure.

perspectives.take: Frames the issue as an unreported external cost of digital infrastructure: operators optimise onsite water use while the grid-linked water consumption of their electricity remains invisible in their disclosures.

articles.title: How data centres consume water for cooling but also to power their energy needs
articles.snippet: Developers may reduce onsite water but do not factor in the water used by the electricity grid where these massive facilities operate.

static.topic: Water footprint of data centres and the energy–water nexus
static.syllabusNode: Environment & Ecology — environmental degradation and resource use; Infrastructure: Energy
static.whatIsIt: Data centres consume water directly in cooling (evaporative cooling towers, chillers) and indirectly through the electricity they draw, since thermal power plants use water for cooling. A full footprint therefore combines onsite water use with offsite, grid-linked water use — the water dimension of what is usually discussed as Scope 2 emissions.
static.background: As cloud computing and AI workloads expanded, operators began reporting onsite water use and adopting Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE) as an efficiency metric. Analysts subsequently noted that improvements at the fence line may not lower total withdrawal if the electricity comes from water-intensive thermal generation.
static.geography: India's data centre clusters are concentrated in and around Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad, Pune and the Noida–Gurugram belt, several of which fall in water-stressed districts.
static.socioEconomic: Industrial water demand competes with agriculture and household supply; states offer land, power and fiscal incentives to attract data centres while absorbing the added local water and electricity demand.
static.whyInNews: Scroll.in reports a study showing that developers may reduce onsite water use but do not factor in the water consumed in generating the electricity that powers these facilities.
static.wayForward: Require disclosure of both onsite and grid-linked water use; mandate treated or recycled water for cooling; factor basin-level water stress into siting approvals; integrate industrial water accounting with state water regulators.
prelimsPointers: WUE measures litres of water consumed per unit of IT load or energy consumed by a data centre.
Thermal power plants are among the largest industrial withdrawers of freshwater, so grid water intensity depends on the generation mix.
India is the world's largest user of groundwater, which makes indirect industrial water demand a basin-level concern.
static.mainsAngle: Efficiency at the fence line is not efficiency for the basin — examine how India's resource governance can account for the indirect water use embedded in industrial electricity consumption.

static.topic: Groundwater and water regulation in India
static.syllabusNode: GS-II: Government policies and interventions; GS-III: Conservation and environmental pollution
static.whatIsIt: Water is Entry 17 of the State List, while inter-state rivers are Entry 56 of the Union List — so regulation is shared but predominantly State-led. Instruments include the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, CPCB and State Pollution Control Boards, and the Central Ground Water Authority for groundwater abstraction.
static.background: The National Water Policy of 1987 was revised in 2012; the Central Ground Water Authority was constituted in 1997 on the direction of the Supreme Court; a Model Groundwater Bill was circulated to states in 2016 and revised thereafter; Atal Bhujal Yojana and Jal Jeevan Mission were launched in 2019; NITI Aayog's Composite Water Management Index was first published in 2018.
static.geography: Water-stressed blocks across Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh overlap with the states attracting large data centre investment.
static.socioEconomic: Industrial users form a small but concentrated and growing share of demand, and permitting and tariffs determine whether they draw freshwater or treated wastewater.
static.whyInNews: The study indicates that a significant part of a data centre's water demand is offsite and therefore largely outside site-level permitting and disclosure.
static.wayForward: Embed water accounting into industrial approvals, make disclosure mandatory, and mandate treated wastewater reuse for cooling in water-stressed areas.
keyTerms: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
prelimsPointers: Water and sanitation are State List subjects (Entry 17); inter-state rivers fall under Entry 56 of the Union List.
The Central Ground Water Authority was constituted in 1997 following a Supreme Court direction.
Under the EIA Notification, 2006, large construction projects above the prescribed built-up area threshold require prior environmental clearance, which can capture large data centre campuses.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether India's water-permitting regime is equipped to capture the indirect, grid-linked water footprint of industry, and suggest institutional reforms.

static.topic: Parliament, legislation and oversight of emerging sectors
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Parliament & Legislative Process
static.whatIsIt: Parliament under Article 79 comprises the President, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. A Bill becomes law after passage by both Houses and Presidential assent under Article 111.
static.background: Money Bills under Article 110 originate only in the Lok Sabha, where the Rajya Sabha may delay but not amend the money provisions; Ordinances under Article 123 may be promulgated when Parliament is not in session and must be approved within six weeks of reassembly; Departmentally Related Standing Committees scrutinise Bills referred to them.
static.whyInNews: Not directly part of the news; included as institutional context, since any statutory framework on data centre water and energy disclosure would have to be enacted by Parliament and would typically be examined by a Departmentally Related Standing Committee.
static.wayForward: Strengthen committee scrutiny of new-economy sectors so that disclosure and efficiency mandates are debated on evidence rather than left entirely to executive policy.
prelimsPointers: A no-confidence motion can be moved only in the Lok Sabha.

Adjournment, prorogation and dissolution differ in their effect on pending Bills; a Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses on dissolution of the Lok Sabha only if it has not yet been passed by the Lok Sabha.
static.mainsAngle: Assess declining legislative scrutiny and committee referrals, and consider how parliamentary productivity shapes regulation of fast-growing sectors.

prelims: Data centres use water both onsite (cooling) and offsite (water consumed in generating the electricity drawn from the grid).
Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE) is the standard onsite efficiency metric for data centre water consumption.
Thermal power plants require water for cooling, so the water intensity of a data centre's electricity depends on the grid's generation mix.
Water is primarily a State subject in India (Entry 17, State List), with groundwater abstraction regulated through the Central Ground Water Authority.
stories.mainsQuestion: Data centres are expanding rapidly in India, but their water footprint extends well beyond their own sites. Examine the adequacy of India's existing water and environmental regulatory framework in accounting for the indirect water use of industry, and suggest reforms.

stories.headline: India's forex reserves fall by more than $14 billion, RBI data show
stories.summary: RBI data show India's foreign exchange reserves fell by more than $14 billion, according to a report by TheWire.in. The decline is significant because reserves are the RBI's key buffer against external shocks and currency volatility. The data do not by themselves establish a single cause; reserve movements can reflect valuation changes, gold prices, and RBI intervention. The development keeps attention on India's import cover and external sector resilience.
stories.whyItMatters: Directly relevant to GS-III external sector, RBI functions, and monetary policy; useful for prelims facts on forex reserves and mains discussions on external stability.

perspectives.take: Reports the RBI data as a neutral news development, highlighting the scale of the decline without attributing causes.

articles.title: Indias Foreign Exchange Reserves Fall by More than $14 Billion, RBI Data Reveals
articles.snippet: Indias Foreign Exchange Reserves Fall by More than $14 Billion, RBI Data Reveals TheWire.in

static.topic: RBI and Forex Reserves Management
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Banking & Monetary Policy; External Sector
static.whatIsIt: The RBI is India's central bank and manager of foreign exchange reserves. Reserves comprise foreign currency assets, gold, Special Drawing Rights, and the reserve tranche position with the IMF.
static.background: The RBI was established in 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934, and nationalised in 1949. It conducts monetary policy through the six-member Monetary Policy Committee since 2016, with a 4% CPI inflation target within a 2–6% band. It also manages forex reserves and publishes weekly data.
static.socioEconomic: Adequate reserves support import cover, exchange-rate stability, and confidence in the external sector; sharp declines can raise concerns about vulnerability to global shocks.
static.whyInNews: RBI data show reserves fell by more than $14 billion, as reported by TheWire.in.
static.wayForward: Monitor reserve adequacy in terms of import cover and short-term debt; maintain buffers against global volatility; ensure transparent communication of reserve movements.
prelimsPointers: RBI manages India's forex reserves and publishes weekly data.
Forex reserves include foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs, and reserve tranche position.
A fall in reserves can reflect valuation effects, gold price changes, or RBI intervention.
static.mainsAngle: Examine the adequacy of India's forex reserves and the policy options to manage external sector shocks.

prelims: RBI data show India's forex reserves fell by more than $14 billion.
Forex reserves are held and managed by the RBI.
Reserve movements can be driven by valuation changes and RBI market intervention.
stories.mainsQuestion: Discuss the role of foreign exchange reserves in ensuring external sector stability. What factors explain sharp fluctuations in India's reserves, and what policy responses are appropriate?

stories.headline: CBIC proposes draft GST changes to shield genuine buyers from ITC loss
stories.summary: The Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) has floated draft amendments to the GST framework aimed at preventing genuine buyers from losing input tax credit (ITC) when their suppliers fail to deposit collected tax. The proposal seeks to distinguish bona fide recipients from collusive or fraudulent claimants, a long-standing pain point under the present system where ITC is denied if the supplier's returns are not reflected in GSTR-2B or tax remains unpaid. It is expected to introduce procedural safeguards, possibly including documentary proof and a mechanism for re-availing credit, reducing litigation and working-capital stress for compliant businesses. The move follows concerns that honest purchasers are penalised for supplier defaults, and will likely require the GST Council's approval before notification.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests the balance between anti-evasion enforcement and ease of doing business under GST; relevant to GS-III taxation, fiscal federalism and GS-II governance.

perspectives.take: Frames the draft as a taxpayer-friendly correction that shields compliant buyers from supplier-side defaults, reflecting a business-paper focus on compliance burden and litigation risk.

articles.title: CBIC proposes draft GST changes to shield genuine buyers from ITC loss
articles.snippet: CBIC proposes draft GST changes to shield genuine buyers from ITC loss Business Standard

static.topic: Goods and Services Tax (GST) and Input Tax Credit
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Taxation; Indirect Tax Reform
static.whatIsIt: GST is a destination-based indirect tax on supply of goods and services, subsuming multiple central and state levies. Input Tax Credit (ITC) allows a registered taxpayer to set off tax paid on inputs against output tax liability, preventing cascading.
static.background: Introduced via the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 and rolled out on 1 July 2017. The GST Council, constituted under Article 279A, is the constitutional body for harmonising rates and rules. ITC is governed by Section 16 of the CGST Act, 2017 and related rules.
static.geography: Applies across India; the GST Council embodies cooperative federalism with Union and state representation.
static.socioEconomic: ITC is critical for working capital of MSMEs and traders; denial on supplier default raises compliance costs and litigation.
static.whyInNews: CBIC has proposed draft GST changes to protect genuine buyers from ITC loss when suppliers default.
static.wayForward: Streamline GSTR-2B/3B matching, provide clear documentary safe harbours for bona fide recipients, and use data analytics to target fraud without burdening compliant taxpayers.
prelimsPointers: GST was launched on 1 July 2017 via the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016.
The GST Council is a constitutional body under Article 279A, chaired by the Union Finance Minister.
ITC is available under Section 16 of the CGST Act, 2017 subject to conditions including payment of tax by the supplier.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how the design of ITC enforcement affects the ease of doing business and federal trust in GST administration.

static.topic: Fiscal Policy, Budget and FRBM
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Government Budgeting
static.whatIsIt: Fiscal policy is the government's use of taxation and spending to steer the economy, presented annually via the Union Budget (Article 112). Fiscal prudence is anchored by the FRBM Act, 2003.
static.background: The FRBM Act targets fiscal-deficit reduction; the N.K. Singh Committee (2017) recommended a debt-to-GDP anchor of 60% (general government). The GST Council (Article 279A) is the constitutional body for indirect-tax harmonisation (GST launched 2017).
static.socioEconomic: GST collections are a key revenue source for both Union and states; ITC disputes affect revenue buoyancy and compliance.
static.whyInNews: CBIC's draft GST amendments touch on indirect tax administration, a component of the broader fiscal framework.
static.wayForward: Balance revenue mobilisation with taxpayer trust; strengthen dispute resolution and data-driven enforcement.
prelimsPointers: Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − total receipts (excluding borrowings).
Finance Commission (Art. 280) recommends tax devolution; 15th FC set 41% share to states.
Defence, interest payments and subsidies dominate committed expenditure.
static.mainsAngle: Debate counter-cyclical capex versus consolidation; examine quality of spending and states' fiscal space.

prelims: CBIC is the apex indirect tax authority under the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance.
Input Tax Credit under GST allows set-off of tax paid on inputs against output tax liability, preventing cascading.
The GST Council, chaired by the Union Finance Minister, is constituted under Article 279A of the Constitution.
Genuine buyers can lose ITC if suppliers fail to file returns or pay tax, a key compliance risk under the present GST regime.
stories.mainsQuestion: The denial of input tax credit to bona fide buyers for supplier defaults undermines the ease of doing business under GST. Critically examine the proposed safeguards and suggest a balanced enforcement framework.

stories.headline: H-1B Delays and New US Rules Push Tech Workers to Leave
stories.summary: Reporting from Washington indicates that processing delays and a tightening set of executive-branch rules on the H-1B programme are prompting a growing number of foreign-born technology professionals to exit the United States or abandon plans to stay. The friction spans both the visa stage and the green-card stage: consular appointments and petition adjudications have slowed, while new conditions and higher costs attached to fresh H-1B filings have raised the effective price of hiring and retaining overseas talent. Indian professionals, who historically account for the largest single share of H-1B recipients, are among the most exposed cohorts, alongside the US technology firms and Indian IT-services exporters that depend on this mobility pipeline. The emerging pattern is being read as a de facto tightening of skilled immigration even without fresh legislation from Congress. It also feeds a wider debate about reverse migration, competitiveness of the US tech sector, and the diversification of Indian talent flows towards Canada, Europe, the Gulf and domestic roles.
stories.whyItMatters: Skilled-mobility policy in the US directly shapes India's services exports, remittance flows and diaspora profile, and is a standing example of how policies of a developed country affect India's interests. It is a high-probability area for questions linking international relations, the Indian diaspora and the domestic technology labour market.

perspectives.take: Frames the story through the Indian talent and IT-services lens — treating the exodus as a cost to Indian professionals and to the India–US mobility corridor rather than as a purely American domestic-policy matter.
Aggregator/curation framing that explicitly credits Bloomberg as the originating reporter, presenting the exodus as a US labour-market and immigration-enforcement story with a business-news angle.

articles.title: H-1B visa delays and Trump's rules force tech workers to leave US

static.topic: H-1B Visa Programme and US Skilled-Immigration Policy
static.syllabusNode: Effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India's interests; Indian Diaspora
static.whatIsIt: The H-1B is a US non-immigrant (temporary work) visa category under the Immigration and Nationality Act, allowing US employers to hire foreign nationals in 'specialty occupations' — roles requiring at least a bachelor's degree or equivalent in a specific field, such as software engineering, mathematics, architecture, medicine, accounting and research. It is employer-sponsored and tied to a certified Labour Condition Application (LCA) filed with the US Department of Labor.
static.background: The H-category of temporary workers was created by the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952; the H-1B 'specialty occupation' sub-category and its numerical cap were shaped decisively by the Immigration Act of 1990. The current annual cap is 65,000 general petitions plus 20,000 reserved for holders of advanced degrees from US institutions, with exemptions for certain cap-exempt employers (higher-education institutions, affiliated non-profits and government research organisations) and for nationals of Chile and Singapore under free-trade commitments. Visas are normally granted for three years and extendable to six; beyond six years continued stay depends on a pending or approved immigrant petition, notably under the AC21 provisions. Selection is by lottery when demand exceeds the cap, administered through an electronic registration system. Policy volatility has been recurrent: the 2017 'Buy American, Hire American' executive order tightened adjudication and raised Requests for Evidence and denials; Proclamation 10052 of June 2020 suspended entry of certain H-1B holders during the pandemic; and in September 2025 a proclamation imposed a payment of US$100,000 on certain new H-1B petitions, while the Department of Homeland Security proposed replacing the random lottery with a selection weighted towards higher wage levels. Dependents travel on H-4 visas, with work authorisation extended to certain H-4 holders under a 2015 rule.
static.geography: United States as the destination economy; India as the single largest source country of H-1B recipients, alongside China, Canada, the Philippines and South Korea.
static.socioEconomic: Indian nationals have historically constituted the largest share of H-1B beneficiaries, commonly estimated at around 70 per cent of cap-subject visas, underpinning Indian IT-services exports, onsite delivery models and a large remittance flow. Tightening raises costs for US employers, lengthens family separation for H-4 dependents, distorts career and education choices of Indian STEM students, and pushes talent towards Canada, the UK, Germany, the Gulf and domestic Indian roles. India has long sought a totalisation agreement with the US to avoid dual social-security contributions by temporary workers.
static.whyInNews: Reports dated November 2026 describe processing delays together with new executive rule changes pushing technology workers to leave the United States, with Indian professionals among the most affected.
static.wayForward: India's options lie in negotiating a bilateral totalisation agreement, pursuing mobility and social-security portability provisions in trade and migration dialogues, expanding domestic high-skill absorption through R&D and deep-tech ecosystems, and diversifying destination markets through mobility partnerships with Canada, the EU, Japan and the Gulf. For the US, the counter-argument is that predictability and a clear high-skill pathway are needed to retain competitiveness.
keyTerms: H-4 dependent visa and H-4 EAD
prelimsPointers: Statutory H-1B cap: 65,000 general visas plus 20,000 for US advanced-degree holders; cap-exempt employers and H-1B1 nationals of Chile and Singapore fall outside it.
Standard validity is three years, extendable to six; the visa is employer-specific and requires a certified LCA from the US Department of Labor.
India is consistently the largest source country for H-1B visas, and dependents are admitted on the H-4 visa.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how shifts in US skilled-immigration policy affect India's services exports, diaspora composition and human-capital strategy, and evaluate the instruments available to India to protect mobility interests.

static.topic: Indian Diaspora, Brain Drain and Reverse Migration
static.syllabusNode: Salient features of Indian society; role of diaspora in India's development — also relevant to GS-II on Indian diaspora
static.whatIsIt: The movement of India's skilled and semi-skilled population abroad — historically to the Gulf and the Anglophone West, more recently to Canada, Europe, Australia and East Asia — and the reverse flow of talent back to India or onwards to third countries when destination-country policies tighten.
static.background: Indian emigration has passed through distinct phases: nineteenth-century indenture labour to Mauritius, Fiji, the Caribbean and Natal; post-independence professional migration to the UK and later the US; the Gulf construction and services boom from the 1970s; and the post-1990s IT and STEM wave enabled by the H-1B route and the Y2K technology cycle. The diaspora is now classified as NRIs, Persons of Indian Origin and Overseas Citizens of India, and is a significant source of remittances, investment and soft power. Periods of destination-country restriction — such as the 2017 and 2020 US executive actions — have historically been followed by visible reverse migration and diversification of destinations.
static.geography: Principal corridors: India–US, India–UK, India–Canada, India–Gulf (UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman), India–Australia and India–South-East Asia.
static.socioEconomic: India is among the world's largest recipients of remittances, with the Gulf and North America as the leading corridors. Tightening in a single high-skill destination shifts flows rather than stopping them, but it does affect family structure, gender dynamics in dependent-spouse work rights, and the composition of India's domestic technology labour supply.
static.whyInNews: The reported departure of H-1B-dependent technology workers from the US is a fresh instance of destination-policy-driven reverse migration and destination diversification.
static.wayForward: Strengthen diaspora-welfare mechanisms, negotiate social-security portability, build domestic research and deep-tech capacity to absorb returning talent, and frame migration policy as a two-way mobility partnership rather than a one-way outflow.
prelimsPointers: India is the world's largest recipient of remittances, with the United States and the Gulf as the largest source corridors.
OCI cards are issued to foreign nationals of Indian origin (with limited exceptions), while PIO cards were subsumed into the OCI scheme.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how restrictive immigration policies in developed countries reshape India's diaspora and evaluate the adequacy of India's response in terms of welfare, portability and domestic talent absorption.

static.topic: India–United States Relations: Trade, Technology and Mobility
static.syllabusNode: Bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India's interests
static.whatIsIt: The India–US relationship is a multi-track engagement spanning defence, civil nuclear cooperation, counter-terrorism, trade and investment, and technology and human-capital mobility. Visa policy sits at the intersection of the trade and people-to-people tracks.
static.background: The relationship was re-anchored by the 2005 civil nuclear agreement and the 2008 IAEA safeguards and NSG waivers; it was subsequently broadened through the designation of India as a Major Defence Partner, the 2+2 ministerial dialogue, logistics and communications agreements, and the Initiative on Critical and Emerging Technology launched in 2023. Trade negotiations have repeatedly run alongside disputes over tariffs, digital taxation and professional-visa access, with India consistently raising totalisation and mobility concerns.
static.geography: Bilateral; the Indo-Pacific is the principal strategic theatre of the partnership.
static.socioEconomic: Indian IT services firms are deeply embedded in US enterprise supply chains and are among the largest users of the H-1B route; mobility restrictions raise their onsite delivery costs and accelerate localisation of hiring in the US. Conversely, Indian students are a major cohort in US STEM programmes, and their post-study options are sensitive to the same policy shifts.
static.whyInNews: H-1B delays and rule changes are being read as a stress point in the technology and mobility pillar of the India–US relationship.
static.wayForward: Separate the mobility track from tariff and trade disputes; push for a totalisation agreement and predictable high-skill pathways; and deepen the critical-technology partnership so that the relationship rests on more than one pillar.
keyTerms: Initiative on Critical and Emerging Technology (iCET)
Civil nuclear cooperation and NSG waiver
prelimsPointers: India was designated a Major Defence Partner of the United States in 2016.
The India–US 2+2 ministerial dialogue involves the foreign and defence ministers of both countries.
The civil nuclear agreement was signed in 2005–2008 and involved an IAEA safeguards agreement and an NSG waiver for India.
static.mainsAngle: Assess whether the technology and human-capital mobility pillar of the India–US relationship has become the weakest link, and suggest how India can insulate its interests from periodic policy swings in Washington.

prelims: The H-1B is a US non-immigrant work visa for 'specialty occupations' requiring at least a bachelor's degree or equivalent; it is employer-sponsored and requires a certified Labour Condition Application with the US Department of Labor.

The statutory H-1B cap is 65,000 general petitions plus 20,000 for holders of advanced degrees from US institutions, with exemptions for certain higher-education, non-profit and government research employers and for nationals of Chile and Singapore.
Visas are normally valid for three years and extendable to six; dependents are admitted on H-4 visas, with work authorisation available to certain H-4 holders.
India is the largest single source country for H-1B beneficiaries, making the programme central to Indian IT-services exports and to the India–US mobility corridor.
stories.mainsQuestion: The tightening of the United States' H-1B regime is often described as skilled-immigration policy by executive action rather than by legislation. Examine its implications for India's services exports, diaspora and human-capital strategy, and evaluate the instruments available to India to secure predictable high-skill mobility.

onThisDay.description: U.S. President John F. Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas, Texas, by Lee Harvey Oswald; Governor John Connally was seriously wounded, and Lyndon B. Johnson was sworn in as the 36th President. The event marked a major turning point in Cold War-era American politics.
